seo.title: Fiji Marine Conservation Program | Pacific Discovery
seo.description: Two weeks on Kuata Island, Fiji for 17–22 year olds: earn your SSI Open Water Diver certification, survey and restore coral reefs, and run your own reef research project.

hero.headline: Learn to dive, study the reef and help restore it
hero.intro: Two weeks on Kuata Island in Fiji’s Yasawa group: earn your SSI Open Water Diver certification, survey reef health in a no-take marine protected area, plant coral and run your own research project.

items.title: Dive certification included
items.body: Non-divers train for the SSI Open Water Diver certification in the first days of the program. Certified divers sharpen their survey skills instead.

items.title: Real reef science
items.body: Learn the survey methods marine scientists use, from transects and quadrats to data sheets, and put them to work in a no-take marine protected area.

items.title: Hands-on restoration
items.body: Build coral frames and plant fragments at the coral nursery, join crown-of-thorns removal dives and run a microplastics survey on the island’s beaches.

items.title: Your own research project
items.body: In week two, small teams choose a research question, collect their own data on research dives and present a reef health report to resort staff and village guests.

itinerary.note: This is a guide to what you can expect to do on program. The order in which activities occur might vary. Itineraries are subject to change.

weeks.title: Dive training & reef science
weeks.body:
Bula, welcome to Fiji! You’ll meet your Program Instructors in Nadi for orientation, a safety briefing and our first team session, then take the boat out to Kuata Island in the Yasawa group. Non-divers train for the SSI Open Water Diver certification while certified divers sharpen their survey skills, and everyone learns to identify the fish and corals of the reef.

Then we learn how marine scientists measure reef health, with transects, quadrats and data sheets, and head out for our first surveys in the island’s no-take marine protected area. We build coral frames and plant fragments at the coral nursery, and join a crown-of-thorns removal dive. An evening lecture on bleaching, runoff and overfishing puts it all in context, and each day a different student takes the lead for the group.
weeks.tags: Dive certification, Reef surveys, Coral nursery
weeks.imageAlt: Students in the ocean in Fiji

weeks.title: Village life, research & farewell
weeks.body:
We visit a neighboring village for a sevusevu, the traditional kava welcome, and spend a day at the local school sharing what we’ve learned about the reef. Later we return for a session on fishing practices and closed fishing areas, and run a microplastics survey on the island’s beaches.

In small teams you choose a research question, plan your method and collect your own data on research dives, with a free afternoon to snorkel, kayak or relax. There’s also an optional shark dive. Our final dives fall about 48 hours before flights home for a safe no-fly buffer. On our last full day we analyze the data and present a reef health report to resort staff and village guests, then celebrate with a lovo feast before taking the boat back to Nadi.

day.heading: What a typical day looks like

notes.title: Free time
notes.body: There’s a free afternoon in week two to snorkel, kayak, read on the beach or just rest. Evenings on the island are relaxed.

notes.title: Phones & wifi
notes.body: We encourage flight mode so you stay present. Wifi on the island is limited.

notes.title: Fitness needed
notes.body: Medium activity level. You should be a confident swimmer and comfortable in the water. Expect daily diving or snorkeling and some physical work on the conservation projects.

items.title: Marine science in the field
items.body: Learn reef survey methods from a resident marine biologist and the dive team, then use them to collect real data on reef health.

items.title: Service you can put on your résumé
items.body: Reef surveys, coral restoration and crown-of-thorns removal, plus your own research project and report. You’ll come home with a dive certification and real experience to talk about in college applications, job interviews and scholarship essays.

items.title: Optional college credit
items.body: Earn college credit through the University of Montana. 529 education funds can be used to pay for your credits and your Pacific Discovery program tuition.

faq.heading: Questions we get about this program

items.q: Do I need to know how to scuba dive?
items.a: No. You’ll train for the SSI Open Water Diver certification in the first days of the program. If you’re already certified, you’ll work on survey skills instead. You do need to be comfortable swimming.
The dive center we work with is SSI-affiliated, so you’ll earn the SSI Open Water Diver certification. It’s recognized worldwide, the same way PADI is.

items.q: How fit do I need to be?
items.a: This program has a medium activity level. Expect daily diving or snorkeling and some physical work on the conservation projects. You should be a confident swimmer.
One night in a hostel in Nadi, then twelve nights at a small island eco-resort on Kuata Island, with its own dive center and resident marine biologist.

items.q: Why is there no diving on the last day?
items.a: Divers shouldn’t fly within about 24 hours of their last dive. We finish diving about 48 hours before flights home to give everyone a safe buffer.
By minivan around Nadi, and by boat between the mainland and Kuata Island.

Tuition covers all in-country transport, accommodation, meals, and the activities and entry fees in the itinerary. It doesn't cover international flights, visas, travel insurance, spending money, optional college credit or optional activities.

items.q: How much spending money should I bring?
items.a: About $100 a week for snacks, personal shopping and optional activities like the shark dive. It varies from student to student.

items.q: Can I stay in touch with home?
items.a: Yes. We encourage keeping phones on flight mode so you stay present, and wifi is available where we stay in cities and towns. There will also be a photo album that students and instructors can upload photos and video to, so parents and caregivers can stay up to date.

items.q: Do I need a passport or visa?
items.a: Your passport must be valid for more than 6 months after the program ends. All the information you need in regard to visas will be available in your student portal.

safety.heading: For parents: how we keep students safe

items.title: 24/7 Emergency Line
items.body: Parents, students and instructors can reach a real person at any hour. Every call is logged and passed to our on-call staff member by phone.

items.title: Wilderness First Aid & Live Risk Assessment
items.body: All our instructors hold Wilderness First Aid (WFA) certification and have extensive training in group leadership and risk management.

items.title: Accredited Safety Systems
items.body: Our safety systems are assessed and accredited by the Gap Year Association (USA), Year Out Group (UK) and OutdoorsMark (NZ). Students on Go Overseas voted us one of the top gap year providers for safety.

items.title: Insurance & Health
items.body: Comprehensive travel insurance is required, covering medical costs and emergency evacuation. Check vaccinations with your doctor, and pack a first-aid kit and any personal medication. Our instructors can't legally give students any medication.
